enrichment.short_title: CPR cross-examination after hearsay witness statements
key_facts: During the Douglas v Hello! trial, neither side called Sue Neal or put her witness statements into evidence.
At the close of the defendants' case, Mr Price put both of Miss Neal's statements in as hearsay under CPR 32.5(5).
The claimants then applied under CPR 33.4 to call Miss Neal for cross-examination on the contents of those statements.
Lindsay J granted the application; the defendants appealed on an interlocutory basis during the adjourned trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal to the Court of Appeal from Lindsay J during the ongoing Hello! privacy trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the judge's order permitting cross-examination of Miss Neal was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party relies on another party's unused witness statement as hearsay under CPR 32.5(5) without calling the maker, CPR 33.4 empowers the court to permit the other party to call and cross-examine the statement-maker on the contents of the statement.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 33.4 applies where the party putting in hearsay did not prepare the witness statement
Interaction of CPR 32.5(5) and CPR 33.4
Scope of cross-examination permitted under CPR 33.4
Whether the defendants could withdraw reliance on Miss Neal's evidence on appeal

confidence.notes: Outcome and CPR-based ratio are explicit; the judgment deliberately avoids setting out the underlying privacy facts.

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 and secure tenancy succession after breach
key_facts: The claimant had lived with her mother in a Brent secure tenancy for over 20 years.
The mother's secure tenancy had ended when she breached a suspended possession order for rent arrears before her death.
Brent refused succession and commenced possession, treating the claimant as a trespasser.
The claimant argued eviction would breach Article 8 and that Brent had failed to conduct a proportionality assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Brent's decision to seek possession after refusing tenancy succession.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; leave to appeal refused; costs order made in favour of the local authority.
enrichment.ratio: Where Parliament's statutory succession scheme, as refined by authority such as Knightley, excludes succession and homeless duties will apply, Article 8 does not ordinarily require a local authority to undertake a case-by-case proportionality review before issuing possession unless the circumstances are exceptional.
legal_issues: Whether eviction engages Article 8 where occupation is not lawfully established
Whether Brent was required to assess proportionality before commencing possession
Effect of Michalak and Sheffield City Council v Smart on housing possession
Whether the County Court could provide an effective Article 8 remedy
index_terms: Brent London Borough Council v Knightley
linked_authorities: Brent London Borough Council v Knightley
Michalak v Wandsworth London Borough Council
Lambeth London Borough Council v Howard

confidence.notes: Outcome and Article 8 ratio follow clearly from the judgment's analysis of Michalak and Smart.

enrichment.short_title: Architect liability for EPS panel fire spread
key_facts: A fire started in Sahib Foods' veg prep area when a gas bratt pan was left on with about 100 mm of oil and a broken thermostat.
The architects had specified combustible EPS sandwich panels in a cooking area despite warnings from the panel supplier LRI.
Fire experts agreed non-combustible compartmentation would have contained the fire within Room G49.
Sahib was negligent in operating the bratt pan; the Co-Op failed to prove latent defects relevant to its claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court liability trial limited to negligence and contributory negligence after a factory fire.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Sahib against the architects for damages to be assessed on a causation basis; Co-Op claim dismissed; no contributory negligence on fire spread.
enrichment.ratio: An architect who knows of the fire risks of EPS panels in food-factory cooking areas breaches the duty of care by proceeding with that specification; where the claimant caused the fire but the defendant should have prevented its spread, damages may be assessed by deducting losses that would have occurred if the fire had been properly contained.
legal_issues: Whether the architects owed duties to Sahib and the Co-Op
Standard of care for architects regarding EPS panels in 1994
Causation of fire initiation versus spread
Apportionment of contributory negligence under the 1945 Act
index_terms: Pride Valley Foods v Hall and Partners
linked_authorities: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee
Bellefield Computer Services v E Turner & Sons
Baxall Securities v Sheard Walshaw Partnership
Pride Valley Foods v Hall and Partners

confidence.notes: Detailed liability findings and the causation-based damages approach are clearly stated in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Licence to occupy and adverse possession after mortgage fraud
key_facts: Miss Farooqui entered possession of a first-floor flat in 1988 as an intending purchaser but completion never occurred after mortgage fraud by the vendor's solicitor.
The county court held she had acquired title by adverse possession from late 1988.
The Court of Appeal held the licence had not terminated before 30 January 1989 because there was no mutual communication that the transaction would not proceed.
Mr Sandhu's possession claim based on a 2000 notice to quit was remitted for further consideration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Central London County Court on adverse possession and possession after an aborted flat purchase.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; adverse possession declaration set aside; possession and licence revocation issues remitted to the county court.
enrichment.ratio: A licence allowing an intending purchaser into possession before completion ends when the parties are no longer proceeding towards completion, but that requires some mutual communication from which an objective observer would infer both appreciate the transaction will not proceed; silent vendor dishonesty does not automatically terminate the licence.
legal_issues: Implied terms of a pre-contract licence to occupy
Whether the licence ended before the 12-year limitation period
Availability of specific performance
Whether a notice to quit validly determined the licence
linked_authorities: J A Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham

confidence.notes: The appeal turned on a clearly articulated implied-term analysis with an explicit order.

enrichment.short_title: MHRT reasons and resection after discharge
key_facts: KW, an 18-year-old, was detained under section 2 for assessment of suspected psychotic illness.
The Mental Health Review Tribunal discharged him without adequate reasons, finding no mental disorder despite Dr O'Connor's evidence.
The NHS Trust immediately resectioned KW under sections 5 and 3.
Both KW's challenge to resection and the Trust's challenge to the discharge were heard together.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated judicial review of MHRT discharge and Trust resection decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal discharge decision quashed and remitted to a fresh tribunal; KW's challenge to resection withdrawn; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: A Mental Health Review Tribunal must give adequate and intelligible reasons when rejecting expert psychiatric evidence under section 72 and rule 23; once an unlawful discharge is quashed it is treated as never having effect, so the patient remains lawfully detained under the prior regime.
legal_issues: Adequacy of MHRT reasons under rule 23(2)
Whether the discharge decision was perverse
Procedural fairness where the medical member's findings were not disclosed
Lawfulness of resection immediately after tribunal discharge
index_terms: R (Von Brandenburg) v East London NHS Trust
linked_authorities: R v MHRT ex p Pickering
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd
R (Von Brandenburg) v East London and City Mental Health NHS Trust

confidence.notes: Grounds one and the quashing order are clearly resolved; costs reasoning is secondary to the core ratio.

enrichment.short_title: Liquidator recovery of unlawful company dividend
key_facts: Marini Ltd, a menswear retailer controlled by the Dickenson family, went into liquidation in July 1999.
On 26 February 1998 the company paid a £120,000 dividend when only £51,772 was available for distribution.
The liquidator sought repayment under section 212 and related insolvency and company law provisions.
Wrongful trading, undervalue car sale and section 317 consultancy fee claims failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery application by the liquidator against former directors and shareholders for misfeasance and related relief.
enrichment.outcome: Partial success: Gary, Gerald and Pauline Dickenson ordered to repay £26,608.92, £6,822.80 and £34,796.28 respectively with interest; other claims dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: An unlawful distribution is recoverable only to the extent it exceeds available distributable profits; section 727 relief should not be granted where directors would retain unlawful payments at creditors' expense; wrongful trading under section 214 requires proof that net asset deficiency worsened after the alleged cut-off date.
legal_issues: Extent of unlawful distribution under Part VIII Companies Act 1985
Availability of section 727 relief for honestly acting directors
Whether section 317 non-disclosure vitiated Earlstar consultancy payments
Section 214 wrongful trading and the net deficiency test
linked_authorities: Bairstow v Queens Moat Houses Plc
Lee Panavision Ltd v Lee Lighting Ltd
MacPherson v European Strategic Bureau Ltd

confidence.notes: Long judgment but the dividend recovery ratio and quantified orders are explicit; some secondary claims add complexity.

enrichment.short_title: Arbitration respondent identity after Saudi reorganisation
key_facts: Hussmann commenced arbitration against Al Ameen Development & Trade Establishment, Mr Pharaon's unincorporated Saudi trading name.
Mr Pharaon later incorporated Al Ameen Development & Trade Co and the tribunal's first award was made in favour of the company.
Thomas J held the company was not a party and set aside the first award as of no effect.
The tribunal then made a second award in favour of Mr Pharaon trading as the Establishment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a deputy High Court judge on challenges under section 67 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to a second arbitral award.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the second award in favour of Mr Pharaon trading as the Establishment was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where arbitration is commenced against the original contract party, an unincorporated establishment, confusion about a later incorporated company does not displace the Establishment as respondent; a tribunal is not functus officio when an earlier merits award is declared of no effect for lack of jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Identity of the respondent to the arbitration reference
Effect of Saudi business transfer without Hussmann's consent
Whether the tribunal was functus officio after the first award
Whether Mr Pharaon was barred from pursuing a second award
linked_authorities: Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council v O'Reilly

confidence.notes: Both issues on appeal were fully reasoned with a clear dismissal order.

enrichment.short_title: FSCS liability for insured employer defence costs
key_facts: Geologistics held a composite business liability policy with Independent Insurance covering employers' liability.
Independent's solicitors DAC defended an employee's personal injury claim but judgment exceeded expectations; Independent entered provisional liquidation.
Geologistics paid DAC's pre-liquidation defence costs of £15,710.55 and sought recovery from the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.
The Scheme accepted liability for the employee's damages and costs but denied liability for the insured's own defence costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Financial Services Compensation Scheme's refusal to pay pre-liquidation defence costs.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declaratory relief granted that Geologistics is entitled to recover pre-liquidation defence costs from the Scheme.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 6(5) of the Policyholders Protection Act 1975, an insured's unsuccessful defence costs incurred in a compulsory employers' liability claim are sufficiently connected to the compulsory liability to fall within full section 6(4) protection rather than being excluded as non-compulsory cover.
legal_issues: Construction of 'in respect of' in section 6(5) PPA 1975
Whether defence costs are covered by compulsory insurance protection
Relationship between sections 6(4) and 6(6)
Policy implications for composite business liability policies
linked_authorities: Scher v Policy Holders Protection Board

confidence.notes: The section 6(5) construction and declaratory outcome are the focused subject of a detailed judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Sudanese draft evader and Article 3 risk
key_facts: The appellant, a Sudanese national from the Nuba region, left Sudan after failing to report for Popular Defence Force training.
The adjudicator dismissed his asylum appeal; the Immigration Appeal Tribunal partially re-decided the case itself.
The IAT found no real risk of identification as a draft evader at Khartoum airport and no real risk of imprisonment or Article 3 ill-treatment.
The Home Office Sudan Country Assessment stated penalties for refusing military service and described harsh prison conditions and security-force abuses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal and immediate Court of Appeal hearing against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT decision set aside and remitted to a differently constituted tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Where the Secretary of State's own country assessment states that refusal of military service carries imprisonment and that security forces commonly torture suspected opponents, the evidential burden shifts to the Secretary of State to show no real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment; the IAT could not require the appellant to prove enforcement of the penalty law in those circumstances.
legal_issues: Real risk of identification as a draft evader at Khartoum airport
Whether prescribed penalties for refusing military service would be imposed
Article 3 risk for a Nuba draft evader
Allocation of evidential burden where Home Office country evidence is relied on

confidence.notes: The Article 3 ratio and remittal order are clearly expressed; refugee convention issues were not pursued on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: SEND Tribunal appeal on ADHD school placement
key_facts: D, a high-functioning child with ADHD and mild dyspraxia, had left mainstream primary school and attended the New Learning Centre at his parents' expense.
Brent's April 2002 statement proposed a mainstream placement at Kensal Rise Primary with 0.6 learning support.
The parents appealed, seeking continued placement at the New Learning Centre and amended descriptions of D's needs.
The SEND Tribunal amended Part 2 on dyspraxia but upheld the Kensal Rise placement in Part 4.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal to the Administrative Court from a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal's statement and Kensal Rise placement were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal must determine the special educational provision required under section 324 before naming a school placement; once an appropriate school placement is identified, section 319 does not permit non-school provision unless the tribunal finds school provision inappropriate.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal adequately addressed required special educational provision in Part 3
Correct sequencing of Part 3 and Part 4 decisions
Meaning of 'appropriate' school under section 324
Procedural fairness and reasons on dyspraxia wording in Part 2
linked_authorities: T v Special Educational Needs Tribunal v Wiltshire County Council
R v Kingston upon Thames Council ex p Hunter
S v Special Educational Needs Tribunal and City of Westminster

confidence.notes: Multiple grounds were considered but the section 319 gateway principle provides a clear central ratio.
